title: Spring Lecture #36: DB Authentication & Password Security
sources: code/springPracticalDemo (User, Role, UserRepository, AuthService, UserController, SecurityConfig)

questions.question: Why do the notes reject encrypting stored passwords and choose a one-way hash instead?
options: Encryption makes the password column too long for MySQL
The application never needs the original password back, and reversible encryption means anyone with the database and the key can recover every password
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared with `PasswordEncoder.matches()` at all, so login would be impossible
Encryption is slower than hashing, which makes login too slow
questions.explanation: Login only has to check whether the entered password matches the registered one, so the original never needs to be recovered. Encryption is reversible: if the database and key leak together, all passwords are exposed. Speed is not the argument; in fact, password hashing is deliberately made slow.
questions.source: notes p14-15 (Why password encryption is not the right solution)

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: true true true
false false false
false true true
true true false
questions.explanation: Each `encode()` call uses a new random salt, so the two encoded strings differ and `equals` is false. `matches()` reads the salt and cost from the stored value and verifies the raw password with them, so both checks return true.
questions.source: notes p18-19 (Salt and BCrypt, practical demonstration)

questions.question: SHA-256 is a secure one-way cryptographic hash. Why is it still a poor choice for storing passwords?
options: It is designed to be fast, so an attacker with a stolen hash database can test huge numbers of guesses offline; adaptive functions like BCrypt make every guess expensive
SHA-256 output can be decrypted with the server's private key
SHA-256 produces different output every time for the same input, so logins fail randomly
SHA-256 is not supported by Java, so it needs an external library
questions.explanation: The weakness is speed: modern hardware computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, which makes offline guessing cheap. Adaptive password functions have a tunable work factor so each guess costs real computation. SHA-256 is deterministic and not reversible, so the other options describe it wrongly.
questions.source: notes p16 (Why a fast hash such as SHA-256 is not enough)

questions.question: A teammate rewrites the lecture's login check like this. Users registered through `register()` (which stores `passwordEncoder.encode(raw)`) now report that login fails even with the correct password. Why?
options: `findByUsername` returns the user without the password column loaded
`equals` is case-sensitive, and BCrypt output uses mixed case
BCrypt cannot encode the same password twice in one JVM
Re-encoding uses a fresh random salt, so the new string never equals the stored one; it must use `passwordEncoder.matches(dto.getPassword(), user.getPassword())`
questions.explanation: Every `encode()` generates a new salt, so comparing two encodings with `equals` is false even for the right password. `matches()` is the correct operation: it takes the salt and parameters from the stored value and verifies the raw password against it, exactly as the lecture's `AuthService.login` does.
questions.source: notes p19 (How does matches() work); code: AuthService.login

questions.question: Your company's users live in an `employees` table with columns `corporate_email`, `credential_hash` and `active`. How does Spring Security authenticate against this table, according to the lecture?
options: Rename the table to `users` and the columns to `username`/`password`, because Spring Security reads those names directly
Provide a `UserDetailsService` that loads the employee through a repository and adapts it to `UserDetails` (email as the username, hash as the password, `active` as enabled)
Make the `Employee` entity extend `InMemoryUserDetailsManager`
Spring Security cannot use custom tables; you must use LDAP or an external identity provider
questions.explanation: Spring Security does not depend on any table design; it works with the `UserDetails` abstraction. A `UserDetailsService` is the bridge that loads the application's own entity and adapts it, and the 'username' can be any unique login identifier such as an email. Renaming the schema is unnecessary.
questions.source: notes p3-5, p12-13 (UserDetails, missing bridge UserDetailsService)

questions.question: Company policy: passwords must be changed every 90 days, but the account itself stays valid. Rohit's password is 95 days old. Which `UserDetails` method should return `false` for him?
options: `isEnabled()`
`isAccountNonExpired()`
`isCredentialsNonExpired()`
`isAccountNonLocked()`
questions.explanation: Credentials-expired means the account is still valid but its credential must be renewed. `isAccountNonExpired()` is for the account itself ending (e.g. a contract), `isAccountNonLocked()` for temporary blocks such as after repeated failed logins, and `isEnabled()` for an account that is deactivated altogether.
questions.source: notes p6-8 (Disabled vs locked, account and credential expiration)

questions.question: This is the lecture's `AuthService.login` (exposed as `POST /api/users/login`, returning `ResponseEntity.ok(loggedIn)`). How do the responses differ for an unknown username and for a known username with a wrong password, and why does that matter?
options: Unknown username: `Optional.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException`, giving a 500 error; wrong password: 200 with `false`. The difference tells an attacker which usernames exist, so both cases should return the same failure
Both return 200 with `false`, because `Optional.get()` returns null for an empty Optional
Both return 401, because Spring Security intercepts failed `matches()` calls
Unknown username: 200 with `false`; wrong password: 500, because `matches()` throws on a mismatch
questions.explanation: `Optional.get()` on an empty Optional throws `NoSuchElementException`, which becomes a server error, while a wrong password just makes `matches()` return false. Responding differently leaks account existence, the enumeration problem from the previous lecture. A safer version treats 'not found' and 'wrong password' identically.

questions.question: During a migration review, someone proposes adding a `password_salt` column next to the BCrypt `password` column "so that matches() can find each user's salt". What is the correct response?
options: Agree: without a salt column every user shares the same salt
Agree: `matches()` takes the salt as a third argument
Disagree, because BCrypt does not use salts; it relies only on its work factor
Disagree: the standard BCrypt string (e.g. `$2a$10$...`) already embeds the algorithm version, cost and salt, and `matches()` reads them from it
questions.explanation: BCrypt is salted, and its encoded output carries the version, cost factor and salt together with the hash. That is why `matches(raw, stored)` needs only two arguments and why a separate salt column is not required. Each user still gets a unique random salt generated at `encode()` time.

questions.question: Using the lecture's `User` entity (`@Column(nullable = false, unique = true) private String username;`, schema created by `ddl-auto=update`) and its `register` method below, `POST /api/users/register` is called twice with username `aditya`. What happens on the second call?
options: A second `aditya` row is inserted, because the passwords hash differently

The INSERT violates the unique constraint on `username`, so `save()` fails with a data-integrity exception and the client gets an error instead of a clean message; the notes add an `existsByUsername` check first
Spring Data's `save()` sees the same username and updates the existing user's password
The request succeeds with "User saved Successfully" but nothing is written
questions.explanation: `save()` on a new entity (null id) calls `persist`, which inserts a row; the database rejects the duplicate `username` because of the unique constraint, and Spring surfaces it as a `DataIntegrityViolationException`. `save()` decides insert vs merge by the id, not by the username. The notes' `AuthService` checks `existsByUsername` first to fail with a clear message.
questions.source: code: AuthService.register, User.java; notes p4-5, p21-23 (Registration service)

questions.question: To enforce 'minimum 8 characters', a developer puts `@Size(min = 8)` on the `password` field of the `User` entity instead of on the registration DTO. Users registering with the password `abc` are accepted. Why?
options: The entity stores the BCrypt-encoded value (about 60 characters), so any password passes the length check; validation must be applied to the raw password in the request DTO before encoding
`@Size` only works on `List` fields, not on `String`
BCrypt pads short passwords to 8 characters before hashing
Bean Validation is disabled whenever Spring Security is on the classpath
questions.explanation: The notes separate validation (is the submitted password acceptable?) from encoding (protecting the stored representation). By the time the entity is validated it holds the encoded hash, which always has a fixed long length. The rule belongs on the raw value, e.g. `@NotBlank @Size(min = 8)` in `RegisterRequest`.
questions.source: notes p21 (Registration DTO: validation vs encoding)
